title: Grace before meals
hook: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts

segments.voice: Yesterday, votive candles: a nurse lighting one after a night shift, and a flame that stays when she goes. Your line was the candle keeps praying.

Tuesday night. Spaghetti, again. A seven-year-old has his fork halfway to his mouth when his grandmother clears her throat. He freezes, puts the fork down, and sighs. Everyone makes the sign of the cross, some faster than others. Then, together, in about the time it takes the steam to rise off the plates, they say it. Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Fork back up. Someone asks for the parmesan. It's over so fast it's easy to miss what was just said.
screen: `A FORK HALFWAY UP.` → `A GRANDMOTHER CLEARS HER THROAT.` → `SAID IN THE TIME STEAM RISES.`

segments.voice: That's the table grace in a traditional English form. You met it in your second week, at a grandmother's table. Today, slowly: four short phrases. First, bless us. Not the food first. The people: the ones at the table, tired, hungry, maybe annoyed with each other. Second, these thy gifts. The spaghetti was bought at a store, cooked by someone's tired hands, paid for with someone's work. All true. And the prayer still calls it a gift, from God, before it's anything else. It quietly rearranges the plate. Third, which we are about to receive. Receive, not take. You can't earn a gift; you can only accept it. And from thy bounty: from God's generosity, which is bigger than this meal. Fourth, through Christ our Lord. The prayer goes through Jesus, who did this himself. In Mark's Gospel, a huge hungry crowd has followed him into a deserted place, and the disciples want to send them away to buy food. Instead he takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the loaves, and gives them to be shared. Everyone eats. Some readers see grace at the table as copying that gesture: look up, bless, then share. Some families add grace after meals too, a short thanks when the plates are empty. Before or after, the point is the same. The food was a gift.
screen: `BLESS US: THE PEOPLE FIRST.` · `THESE THY GIFTS.` · `RECEIVE, NOT TAKE.` · `HE LOOKED UP, BLESSED, AND BROKE.` · then, large: `FROM THY BOUNTY.`

segments.voice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a sandwich at a desk, a bowl of cereal, dinner with people you love, and the hands it passed through: the grower, the driver, the cook. Then picture pausing for one breath before the first bite. If you pray, say the grace slowly, letting each phrase land; if you don't, just pause and notice where the food came from.
Grace before meals. A short blessing said at the table, asking God to bless the people and calling the food his gift. Today's word.
Your line: these thy gifts. Four short phrases, and the plate looks different. That's day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholic families make the sign of the cross and say the traditional grace, "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," together before meals at home and sometimes in restaurants; some also say a grace after meals.

original.script: Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona
original.say: beh-NEH-deek, DOH-mee-neh, nohs et hek TOO-ah DOH-nah
original.note: Latin: the traditional table grace, bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quick formula kids rush through before dinner.
what it means: four phrases that bless the people, call the food God's gift, receive it, and pray through Christ.
what a scholar hears: the Latin Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona, echoing Jesus who looked up, blessed and broke the loaves (Mark 6:41).
guess: a short table prayer calling the food God's gift

chat.says: Why do we say grace? Mom bought the spaghetti at the store.
options: She did, and the prayer still calls it God's gift first: bless us, and these thy gifts.
Grace is mostly a way to thank Grandma for cooking; God isn't really part of it.
Grace makes the food holy, like Communion, so we can't ever skip it.
chat.meaning: The spaghetti was bought and cooked by people, all true, and the prayer still calls it God's gift before anything else.

bounty.meaning: generosity; here, God's, which is bigger than this meal

sign of the cross.meaning: tracing a cross on yourself: forehead, chest, then shoulders

notes: Mark 6:35–44 paraphrased: disciples suggest sending the crowd away to buy food; Jesus takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks and gives. 'Five loaves and two fishes' is stated in the cited text.
Latin form 'Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona quae de tua largitate sumus sumpturi, per Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.' Confirm wording and pronunciation; only the opening is used.
Grace after meals mentioned but not quoted.
